sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: A random sample of 50 students has a mean study time of $\bar{x}=6.2$ hours per week, with sample standard deviation $s=1.8$ hours. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean study time, using a critical value of $z^*\approx1.96$.
questions.answer: Standard error: $\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}=\frac{1.8}{\sqrt{50}}\approx0.255$. Margin of error: $1.96(0.255)\approx0.499$. Confidence interval: $6.2\pm0.499$, or approximately $(5.70, 6.70)$ hours.
questions.explanation: Standard error: $\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}=\frac{1.8}{\sqrt{50}}\approx0.255$. Margin of error: $1.96(0.255)\approx0.499$. Confidence interval: $6.2\pm0.499$, or approximately $(5.70, 6.70)$ hours.

questions.q: Interpret the confidence interval from the previous problem in the context of the study time question, using correct statistical language.
questions.answer: We are 95% confident that the true mean weekly study time for the population of all students is between approximately $5.70$ and $6.70$ hours — meaning that if we repeated this sampling process many times, about 95% of the resulting confidence intervals would capture the true population mean.
questions.explanation: We are 95% confident that the true mean weekly study time for the population of all students is between approximately $5.70$ and $6.70$ hours — meaning that if we repeated this sampling process many times, about 95% of the resulting confidence intervals would capture the true population mean.

questions.q: Explain two ways to decrease the margin of error of a confidence interval, and state a tradeoff involved with each.
questions.target: Margin of error and sample size
questions.answer: (1) Increase the sample size $n$: since margin of error is proportional to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, a larger sample shrinks the margin of error, but larger samples cost more time and resources to collect. (2) Decrease the confidence level (e.g. from 95% to 90%): a lower confidence level uses a smaller critical value, shrinking the margin of error, but this means being less confident that the interval actually captures the true parameter.
questions.explanation: (1) Increase the sample size $n$: since margin of error is proportional to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, a larger sample shrinks the margin of error, but larger samples cost more time and resources to collect. (2) Decrease the confidence level (e.g. from 95% to 90%): a lower confidence level uses a smaller critical value, shrinking the margin of error, but this means being less confident that the interval actually captures the true parameter.

questions.q: State the null hypothesis $H_0$ and alternative hypothesis $H_a$ for a test of whether a coin is biased toward heads (true proportion of heads $p$), and classify the test as one-tailed or two-tailed.
questions.answer: $H_0: p=0.5$ (the coin is fair). $H_a: p>0.5$ (the coin is biased toward heads). This is a one-tailed (right-tailed) test, since the alternative specifies a direction.
questions.explanation: $H_0: p=0.5$ (the coin is fair). $H_a: p>0.5$ (the coin is biased toward heads). This is a one-tailed (right-tailed) test, since the alternative specifies a direction.

questions.q: Explain what a $p$-value represents, in the context of a hypothesis test.
questions.answer: The $p$-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. A small $p$-value suggests the observed data would be unusual if $H_0$ were true, providing evidence against $H_0$.
questions.explanation: The $p$-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. A small $p$-value suggests the observed data would be unusual if $H_0$ were true, providing evidence against $H_0$.

questions.q: A manufacturer claims their light bulbs last on average $\mu=1000$ hours. A sample of 40 bulbs has mean lifetime $\bar{x}=985$ hours with sample standard deviation $s=45$ hours. State the hypotheses and compute the test statistic for testing whether the true mean lifetime is less than claimed.
Using the test statistic $z\approx-2.11$ from the previous problem and a $p$-value of approximately $0.017$, state a conclusion at the $\alpha=0.05$ significance level.
questions.answer: Since the $p$-value ($0.017$) is less than $\alpha=0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is convincing statistical evidence that the true mean bulb lifetime is less than the manufacturer's claimed $1000$ hours.
questions.explanation: Since the $p$-value ($0.017$) is less than $\alpha=0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is convincing statistical evidence that the true mean bulb lifetime is less than the manufacturer's claimed $1000$ hours.

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: In the light bulb test above, describe what a Type I error would mean in context, and what a Type II error would mean in context.
questions.target: Type I and Type II errors, and power
questions.answer: A Type I error would mean concluding the true mean lifetime is less than $1000$ hours when it actually is not (rejecting a true $H_0$) — wrongly penalizing the manufacturer. A Type II error would mean failing to detect that the true mean lifetime really is less than $1000$ hours (failing to reject a false $H_0$) — missing a real problem with the bulbs.
questions.explanation: A Type I error would mean concluding the true mean lifetime is less than $1000$ hours when it actually is not (rejecting a true $H_0$) — wrongly penalizing the manufacturer. A Type II error would mean failing to detect that the true mean lifetime really is less than $1000$ hours (failing to reject a false $H_0$) — missing a real problem with the bulbs.

questions.q: Explain what the power of a test measures, and state one way to increase it.
questions.target: Type I and Type II errors, and power
questions.answer: Power measures the probability that a test correctly rejects $H_0$ when the alternative hypothesis is actually true (i.e. correctly detecting a real effect). Power can be increased by increasing the sample size, which reduces variability in the sampling distribution and makes real effects easier to detect.
questions.explanation: Power measures the probability that a test correctly rejects $H_0$ when the alternative hypothesis is actually true (i.e. correctly detecting a real effect). Power can be increased by increasing the sample size, which reduces variability in the sampling distribution and makes real effects easier to detect.

questions.q: A poll of 400 randomly selected voters finds that 220 support a candidate. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the true population proportion, using $z^*\approx1.96$.
questions.answer: $\hat{p}=\frac{220}{400}=0.55$. Standard error: $\sqrt{\frac{0.55(0.45)}{400}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.2475}{400}}\approx0.0249$. Margin of error: $1.96(0.0249)\approx0.0488$. Confidence interval: $0.55\pm0.0488$, or approximately $(0.501,0.599)$.
questions.explanation: $\hat{p}=\frac{220}{400}=0.55$. Standard error: $\sqrt{\frac{0.55(0.45)}{400}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.2475}{400}}\approx0.0249$. Margin of error: $1.96(0.0249)\approx0.0488$. Confidence interval: $0.55\pm0.0488$, or approximately $(0.501,0.599)$.

questions.q: A researcher wants a margin of error of at most $0.03$ for a 95% confidence interval for a population proportion, using a conservative planning value of $p=0.5$ (which maximizes required sample size). Find the minimum sample size needed, using $n=\left(\frac{z^*}{m}\right)^2p(1-p)$ with $z^*=1.96$.
questions.target: Determining sample size for a target margin of error
questions.answer: $n=\left(\frac{1.96}{0.03}\right)^2(0.5)(0.5)=(65.33)^2(0.25)\approx4268.4(0.25)\approx1067.1$. Round up: $n=1068$ (sample size must always be rounded up to guarantee the margin of error requirement is met).
questions.explanation: $n=\left(\frac{1.96}{0.03}\right)^2(0.5)(0.5)=(65.33)^2(0.25)\approx4268.4(0.25)\approx1067.1$. Round up: $n=1068$ (sample size must always be rounded up to guarantee the margin of error requirement is met).

questions.q: A nutritionist claims a new granola bar has a mean of $200$ calories. A sample of 15 bars has mean $\bar{x}=206$ calories with sample standard deviation $s=9$ calories. Since the population standard deviation is unknown and $n$ is small, a $t$-test is used. Compute the test statistic $t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}$.
Explain what it means for a hypothesis test result to be "statistically significant," and why statistical significance does not always imply practical importance.
questions.answer: A result is statistically significant when the $p$-value is small enough (below the chosen $\alpha$) to reject $H_0$, meaning the observed data would be unlikely if $H_0$ were true. However, with a very large sample size, even a tiny, practically unimportant difference can become statistically significant — so significance alone doesn't guarantee the effect is large or meaningful in real-world terms; the actual size of the effect should also be considered.
questions.explanation: A result is statistically significant when the $p$-value is small enough (below the chosen $\alpha$) to reject $H_0$, meaning the observed data would be unlikely if $H_0$ were true. However, with a very large sample size, even a tiny, practically unimportant difference can become statistically significant — so significance alone doesn't guarantee the effect is large or meaningful in real-world terms; the actual size of the effect should also be considered.

questions.q: A researcher wants to test whether a new fitness program changes the average resting heart rate of participants from the population baseline of $\mu=72$ bpm. A sample of 36 participants after the program has mean resting heart rate $\bar{x}=68.5$ bpm with sample standard deviation $s=10.5$ bpm. State the hypotheses (choosing a two-sided alternative), compute the test statistic, and using a $p$-value of approximately $0.11$, state a conclusion at $\alpha=0.05$.
questions.answer: $H_0:\mu=72$. $H_a:\mu\neq72$. Test statistic: $t=\frac{68.5-72}{10.5/\sqrt{36}}=\frac{-3.5}{1.75}=-2.0$. Since the $p$-value ($0.11$) is greater than $\alpha=0.05$, we fail to reject $H_0$ — there is not enough evidence that the fitness program changes the average resting heart rate.
questions.explanation: $H_0:\mu=72$. $H_a:\mu\neq72$. Test statistic: $t=\frac{68.5-72}{10.5/\sqrt{36}}=\frac{-3.5}{1.75}=-2.0$. Since the $p$-value ($0.11$) is greater than $\alpha=0.05$, we fail to reject $H_0$ — there is not enough evidence that the fitness program changes the average resting heart rate.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: Explain the relationship between a confidence interval and a two-sided hypothesis test at the same confidence/significance level — specifically, describe how you could use a 95% confidence interval alone to decide whether to reject $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ at $\alpha=0.05$, without separately computing a $p$-value.
questions.answer: A 95% confidence interval and a two-sided test at $\alpha=0.05$ are directly linked: if the hypothesized value $\mu_0$ falls outside the 95% confidence interval, then $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ would be rejected at $\alpha=0.05$; if $\mu_0$ falls inside the confidence interval, $H_0$ would fail to be rejected. This means a confidence interval can be used as a quick visual/numeric check for significance without needing to separately calculate a $p$-value.
questions.explanation: A 95% confidence interval and a two-sided test at $\alpha=0.05$ are directly linked: if the hypothesized value $\mu_0$ falls outside the 95% confidence interval, then $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ would be rejected at $\alpha=0.05$; if $\mu_0$ falls inside the confidence interval, $H_0$ would fail to be rejected. This means a confidence interval can be used as a quick visual/numeric check for significance without needing to separately calculate a $p$-value.

questions.q: A restaurant chain wants to test whether a new menu item's average preparation time is longer than the target of 8 minutes, since customers have complained about slow service. A random sample of 30 orders for the new item has a mean preparation time of $\bar{x}=8.7$ minutes with sample standard deviation $s=1.8$ minutes. State the hypotheses for this one-sided test, compute the test statistic, and using a $p$-value of approximately $0.019$, state a conclusion at $\alpha=0.05$ in the context of the restaurant's concern.
questions.answer: $H_0:\mu=8$. $H_a:\mu>8$. Test statistic: $t=\frac{8.7-8}{1.8/\sqrt{30}}=\frac{0.7}{0.329}\approx2.13$. Since the $p$-value ($0.019$) is less than $\alpha=0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is convincing statistical evidence that the true mean preparation time for the new menu item exceeds the 8-minute target, supporting the customers' complaints about slow service.
questions.explanation: $H_0:\mu=8$. $H_a:\mu>8$. Test statistic: $t=\frac{8.7-8}{1.8/\sqrt{30}}=\frac{0.7}{0.329}\approx2.13$. questions.q: An agricultural researcher is designing an experiment to study the yield of a new variety of wheat. The experiment investigates two factors: - Factor 1: Fertilizer formula, with $3$ different types. - Factor 2: Watering frequency, with $4$ different schedules. If the experiment uses a completely randomized design where each subject receives a combination of one fertilizer formula and one watering schedule, how many distinct treatment groups are there?
questions.answer: In an experiment with multiple factors, a treatment is a specific combination of levels of each factor. 1. Identify the number of levels for each factor: - Factor 1 (Fertilizer) has $3$ levels. - Factor 2 (Watering) has $4$ levels. 2. Apply the multiplication counting principle to find the total number of distinct treatment combinations: $\mathrm{Number\ of\ treatments} = 3 \times 4 = 12$ - Choosing $7$ is a common misconception resulting from adding the levels of the factors ($3 + 4$) rather than multiplying them. - Choosing $64$ results from inappropriately raising one number of levels to the power of the other ($4^3$). Final Answer: $12$
questions.explanation: In an experiment with multiple factors, a treatment is a specific combination of levels of each factor. 1. Identify the number of levels for each factor: - Factor 1 (Fertilizer) has $3$ levels. - Factor 2 (Watering) has $4$ levels. 2. questions.q: A study investigates the effectiveness of a new teaching method by comparing the test scores of students who used the new method versus those who used the traditional method. The results are summarized in a two-way table. If the table has $4$ rows and $3$ columns, what is the degrees of freedom (df) for a chi-square test of homogeneity?
questions.target: Determining sample size for a target margin of error
questions.answer: For a chi-square test of homogeneity or independence with a two-way table, the degrees of freedom (df) are calculated using the formula: $\mathrm{df} = (r-1)(c-1)$, where $r$ is the number of rows and $c$ is the number of columns. In this case, the number of rows is $r = 4$ and the number of columns is $c = 3$. Substituting these values into the formula: $\mathrm{df} = (4-1)(3-1) = (3)(2) = 6$. Therefore, the degrees of freedom are 6.
questions.explanation: For a chi-square test of homogeneity or independence with a two-way table, the degrees of freedom (df) are calculated using the formula: $\mathrm{df} = (r-1)(c-1)$, where $r$ is the number of rows and $c$ is the number of columns. In this case, the number of rows is $r = 4$ and the number of columns is $c = 3$. Substituting these values into the formula: $\mathrm{df} = (4-1)(3-1) = (3)(2) = 6$. Therefore, the degrees of freedom are 6.

questions.q: A researcher is conducting a survey on the relationship between college major and career satisfaction. They collected data from $150$ students and organized it into a two-way table. If the number of rows in the table represents $3$ different college majors and the number of columns represents $5$ different levels of career satisfaction, what is the $\mathrm{df}$ for a chi-square test of independence?
questions.answer: For a chi-square test of independence, the degrees of freedom ($\mathrm{df}$) are calculated using the formula $\mathrm{df} = (r - 1)(c - 1)$, where $r$ is the number of rows and $c$ is the number of columns in the contingency table. In this case, $r = 3$ (college majors) and $c = 5$ (career satisfaction levels). Therefore, $\mathrm{df} = (3 - 1)(5 - 1) = (2)(4) = 8$.
questions.explanation: For a chi-square test of independence, the degrees of freedom ($\mathrm{df}$) are calculated using the formula $\mathrm{df} = (r - 1)(c - 1)$, where $r$ is the number of rows and $c$ is the number of columns in the contingency table. In this case, $r = 3$ (college majors) and $c = 5$ (career satisfaction levels). Therefore, $\mathrm{df} = (3 - 1)(5 - 1) = (2)(4) = 8$.

questions.q: What is the correct interpretation of a $95\%$ confidence interval for a population mean $(42.1, 48.7)$?
choices: We are $95\%$ confident that the true population mean falls between $42.1$ and $48.7$
There is a $95\%$ probability that the true mean is between $42.1$ and $48.7$
$95\%$ of all individual values in the population lie between $42.1$ and $48.7$
$95\%$ of sample means will equal the population mean
questions.answer: Confidence level refers to the long-run success rate of the method: in repeated sampling, $95\%$ of intervals generated will capture the fixed true parameter.

questions.q: How can you decrease the width of a confidence interval?
choices: Increase the sample size or decrease the confidence level
Increase the confidence level or increase the sample size
Decrease the sample size or increase the confidence level
Increase the standard deviation of the data
questions.answer: Width is $2 \times \mathrm{critical\ value} \times \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. Increasing $n$ shrinks the denominator; lowering confidence level (e.g. from $99\%$ to $90\%$) lowers the critical value.

questions.q: Why do statisticians state 'fail to reject $H_0$' instead of 'accept $H_0$'?
choices: Failing to find sufficient evidence against $H_0$ does not prove that $H_0$ is true
Because $H_0$ is always false in practice
To avoid computing the test statistic
Because the P-value is always approximate
questions.answer: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; we never prove the null hypothesis true, we merely conclude the data is consistent with it.

questions.q: What is a Type II error?
questions.target: Type I Error, Type II Error, and Power
choices: Failing to reject the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually false
Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
questions.answer: A Type II error (probability $\beta$) is a false negative: failing to detect a real effect when the alternative hypothesis is true.

questions.q: When estimating a population mean $\mu$ with unknown $\sigma$, which distribution and test statistic are used?
